name: Whole30

card.summary: A 30-day strict elimination diet of sugar, grains, dairy, alcohol and legumes; popular as a reset, with no controlled trials of its own.
card.note: Dietitians have criticised its restrictiveness; no studies of the program's health effects.

quick.overview:
Whole30 asks participants to eat only whole foods for 30 days, cutting added sugar, alcohol, grains, dairy and legumes, then to reintroduce them one by one. Its founders frame it as a reset for energy, digestion and cravings.

It is used in appearance circles as a clean-eating protocol. Wikipedia notes no studies had examined its health effects, and some dietitians call it too extreme.
quick.mechanism: The premise is that removing common trigger foods and reintroducing them reveals individual sensitivities; any weight change is generally attributed to cutting processed foods.
quick.risks: Critics highlight restrictiveness and exclusion of whole grains and legumes. The program's own materials and independent studies on physical risk are limited.

lead: Whole30 is a 30-day elimination diet created in 2009 by Melissa Hartwig (now Melissa Urban) and Dallas Hartwig. For a month, participants eat meat, seafood, eggs, vegetables, fruit, nuts, seeds and certain fats and leave out added sugar, alcohol, grains, dairy and (in the original version) legumes and soy, then reintroduce those foods one at a time.[1][2]

People use it as a clean-eating reset aimed at looking and feeling better: less bloat and puffiness, fewer cravings, steadier energy and sleep, and for many a leaner physique and clearer-looking skin. The founders themselves frame it as a reset rather than a weight-loss plan and discourage weighing or calorie counting.[1][2]

On T Nation, lifters mention doing Whole30 alongside lifting plans, for example one poster reporting getting leaner while adding some mass to the delts and upper back, and another planning a month of it with high-rep lifting.[4][5] Wikipedia reports that no studies had specifically examined its health effects as of 2019 and that dietitians are divided on its restrictions.[1]

chain: Cut added sugar, alcohol and highly processed foods for 30 days
Fewer excess calories, less bloat, steadier eating habits
Leaner look and, as followers report, clearer skin and better energy
angle.text: Followers use Whole30 as a short, strict clean-eating month to drop bloat and excess processed-food calories and to see how foods affect them. Reported appearance outcomes include a leaner look and clearer skin, mostly self-reported.

paras: Allowed foods are meat, seafood, eggs, vegetables, fruit, nuts, seeds and certain fats. It is stricter than the paleo diet because it also bans honey and maple syrup. Participants are told not to count calories or weigh themselves, and the reintroduction phase tests food groups individually [1][2]. A plant-based version permits legumes and soy [1].

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and fitness communities
paras: T Nation posters discuss Whole30 as a version of paleo. One reports doing it with a spouse at moderate carbohydrate intake and getting leaner while adding some mass to the delts and upper back; another plans a one-month Whole30 with a high-rep lifting plan as part of a fat-loss goal.[4][5] A coach on the forum says clients who followed perfect Whole30 or paleo eating got little change when gut health issues were present.[6]

The Hartwigs began the program in April 2009 and co-wrote It Starts with Food (2012) and The Whole30 (2015). They separated in 2015 and Melissa Urban took over the business [1]. A 2016 New York Times article noted over a million Instagram posts using #Whole30, and by 2018 the trademark was licensed to food companies [1]. Grokipedia reports rule updates over time, including allowing white potatoes in 2014 [2].

No studies found. Wikipedia reports that no studies had specifically examined the program's health effects as of 2019.[1] Grokipedia mentions a 2018 pilot study and a survey of completers, which are self-reported and not controlled.[2] A separate modelling study estimated greenhouse gas implications of commercial weight-loss diets, not health effects.[3]

Many dietitians agree with its emphasis on protein, vegetables and avoiding added sugar and alcohol, while some consider it too extreme [1]. David L. Katz criticised excluding whole grains and legumes, saying this conflicts with a large body of evidence [1]. U.S. News and World Report ranked it last of 38 diets in 2016 and 2017, citing restrictiveness and social impact [1].

timeline.event: Whole30 launched by Melissa and Dallas Hartwig [1][2].
The Whole30 book published; founders separate [1].
Trademark licensed to several food companies [1].

lore.intro: Followers describe Whole30 as a one-month reset and share results; the founders emphasise non-scale outcomes. On T Nation it is discussed as paleo-style eating alongside training.[4][5][6]

claims.claim: Thirty days off sugar, grains, dairy and alcohol resets energy, sleep and cravings.
claims.believers: The founders and participants report better energy, sleep and fewer cravings [2].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports no studies had specifically examined the program's health effects as of 2019 [1].

claims.claim: The reintroduction phase identifies personal food sensitivities.
claims.believers: Proponents say reintroducing groups one at a time reveals triggers [2].
claims.experts: No published trial has tested the method; the program is not a validated diagnostic procedure [1].

claims.claim: Excluding legumes and whole grains is necessary.
claims.believers: The founders say these foods may affect gut and inflammation [1].
claims.experts: David Katz has said excluding them conflicts with a large body of evidence [1].

claims.claim: Strict clean eating produces leaner, better-looking results when paired with training.
claims.believers: T Nation posters report getting leaner while adding some muscle in the delts and upper back on a Whole30 approach.[4]
claims.experts: No controlled study of the program's body-composition effects is cited by reference sources.[1]
